agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 carries the superscription 'A psalm of Asaph' (KJV 79:0) together with the first line of the poem. I translated both in one verse as the packet's verse map does. 'Asaph' is the guild name of the temple singers (cf. 1 Chr 25), not necessarily the man of David's time; the psalm itself speaks of the destroyed temple, so a date after 587 BCE is the common reading (though 2 Kings 25 / Jer 52 are my own association, not sourced).

STEPBible glosses 'לעיים' as 'into heaps of ruins'. Literal layer keeps 'into heaps' (plural of ʿi, a ruin-mound); Rashi and Radak read 'gelim' (piles of stones). Micah 3:12 / Jer 26:18 use the same word, but the verse text in the packet does not quote them, so I cite only the commentators.

agent_notes: KJV renders 'tiv'ar' as a question ('shall thy jealousy burn'); YLT as a statement. Hebrew has no question particle: the interrogative carries over from 'ad-mah'. I kept it a question.

Revised after review: the 'el' = 'al' parallel is now 'el heharim lo akhal' (Ezek 18:6), attributed to Meiri; 'el yesod hamizbeach' is attributed to Ibn Ezra. The resemblance to Jer 10:25 is my own observation and carries no source.

The five English versions split on goyim: KJV and Webster 'heathen', the others 'nations'. I kept 'nations' in both layers, because 'heathen' reads the word as religious contempt, while the verse defines the nations by their not knowing YHWH.

agent_notes: 'akhal' is singular ('it/he has devoured'), 'hesham-mu' is plural. KJV, ASV and Webster harmonize both to 'they'. Literal layer keeps the number shift; Meiri reads the singular as the wicked king leading the enemy. Some manuscripts and versions read plural 'akhlu'; I translated the text as it stands.

'avonot rishonim' is genuinely ambiguous: 'iniquities of former ones' (ancestors, so ASV/BBE 'forefathers') or 'former iniquities' (KJV, Radak, Meiri's 'sins of youth'). I kept 'former ones' in the literal layer with a bracket-free ambiguity-preserving rendering 'iniquities of the former [ones]' and explained both in the commentary. Ibn Ezra prefers the ancestors reading.
